newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli cabinet passes budget cut, no new taxes.
newsitem.headline: Israeli cabinet passes budget cut, no new taxes.

text.p: The Israeli cabinet on Monday approved further budget cuts which Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said were needed to put the economy back on track and maintain Israel's financial health.

Government officials said the cabinet voted 14-4 in favour of the 1.2 billion shekel ($366 million) cut in state spending at the end of an eight-hour session. They said no new taxes were included in the budget cut package.
"I am happy that the government approved our proposal almost without change," Finance Minister Dan Meridor told reporters after the vote. "We will not raise the tax rates."

"The train has passed another station, it has not gotten to its final destination. The last station is before us, the debate in the Knesset (Israel's parliament) finance committee and the plenum in the coming weeks," Meridor said.
The cutback comes on top of the 4.9 billion shekels already slashed from the original 1997 budget of 190.8 billion shekels which parliament must ratify before December 31.

"Today, the world is watching us -- investors, banks and governments -- to see...whether the government will fix what has gone wrong in the economy in the last two years," Meridor said before the vote.
Economists said government revenues had fallen below projections and the prospect of increased government borrowing had pushed up interest rates, strengthened the shekel and sucked in imports.
As a result Israel's current account deficit is expected to widen to more than $5 billion this year from $4.1 billion in 1995.

Treasury sources had originally put the additional cutbacks in government spending at 1.8 billion shekels. But Meridor found other sources of income to raise 600 million shekels, bringing the real cut down to 1.2 billion shekels.

The proposal passed by the cabinet states that the additional 600 million shekels includes the sale of 3,000 government-owned homes in the occupied West Bank. The move is certain to draw Arab and international ire.
Netanyahu accused the Labour government which he defeated in May elections of managing the economy "terribly" and said his administration would "correct the financial system".
Former prime minister Shimon Peres dismissed the criticism, telling Israel Radio: "They were four wonderful years for the Israeli economy, it grew like yeast".
Legislators have said the reductions, widely reported to target spending on social welfare and education, would hit lower-income Israelis hardest.
It was not immediately clear if the coalition would muster a majority in the 120-seat parlimanet to pass the budget.
The religious Shas party, which enjoys the support of many low-income Israelis, voted against the budget cut in the cabinet and said it had not yet decided how it would vote in parliament.
If Shas, which holds 10 seats, votes against the cuts it could deny Netanyahu a parliamentary majority.
The ministries, which under the package incurred varying percentages of cuts to their budgets, have until Thursday to determine where they will make the slashes.
The announcement of cabinet approval for the cuts was made after the close of trading on the Tel Aviv stock market.
($1=3.28 shekels)
